items.question: 1,000 shares of ₹10 each, issued at par, were forfeited after the holder paid only ₹5 per share. Of these, 600 shares were reissued at ₹9 per share as fully paid-up. What amount is transferred to Capital Reserve on this reissue?
items.explanation: Capital Reserve is the forfeited amount on the reissued shares, less the discount allowed on reissue. Forfeited amount on 600 shares is ₹3,000. Discount is ₹1 × 600 = ₹600. So ₹3,000 − ₹600 = ₹2,400.

why_not.C: Ignores the discount allowed on reissue; takes full forfeited amount of 600 shares.
why_not.D: Adds the discount to the forfeited amount instead of deducting it.
why_not.A: Uses forfeited amount on all 1,000 shares, though only 600 were reissued.

items.exam_tip: Only the forfeited balance on shares actually reissued, after setting off the reissue loss, goes to Capital Reserve.
items.calculation:
paid = 5
forfeited = paid * 600
discount = (10 - 9) * 600
answer = forfeited - discount

items.question: A company must choose between two projects. Project P gives higher accounting profit in the first year but its profits come late in the next years and are uncertain. Project Q gives lower, steady and earlier cash flows. Which approach favours Q?
options: Wealth maximisation, as it weighs timing and risk of cash flows
Profit maximisation, as it adjusts for risk through EPS
Profit maximisation, as it looks at total accounting profit
Wealth maximisation, as it ignores cash flows beyond one year
items.explanation: Wealth maximisation uses discounted cash flows, so timing (time value) and risk are both considered. Earlier, steadier cash flows have higher present value, so Q can be preferred even if P shows higher profit.

why_not.C: Profit maximisation ignores time value and risk, so it would favour P, not Q.
why_not.B: EPS does not adjust for risk or timing; this is a common false belief.
why_not.D: Wealth maximisation looks at all future cash flows, not one year only.

items.exam_tip: Profit max: no time value, no risk, vague meaning. Wealth max: discounted cash flows adjusted for risk.
check_notes: Checker: Option A is much longer and more complete than the others, which may hint that it is correct.
Checker: The stem says P's profits come 'late in the next years' but doesn't say whether P's total profit exceeds Q's. This makes C weaker, but it doesn't create a second defensible answer.

items.question: Under Ind AS 103, on 1 October 2026 Alfa Ltd buys 80% of Beta Ltd for ₹4,40,00,000 cash. Fair value of Beta's identifiable net assets is ₹5,00,00,000. NCI's fair value is ₹1,05,00,000. Acquisition costs paid were ₹6,00,000. NCI is measured at fair value. Goodwill is?
items.explanation: Goodwill = consideration + NCI at fair value − fair value of identifiable net assets. Acquisition-related costs are expensed in profit or loss under Ind AS 103, not added to goodwill.

working.label: Less: Net assets at fair value

why_not.A: Capitalised the ₹6,00,000 acquisition costs into goodwill; they are expensed.
why_not.B: Measured NCI at proportionate share (₹1,00,00,000) though fair value was stated.
why_not.D: Ignored NCI and compared consideration with full net assets, getting a gain.

items.exam_tip: Full goodwill method: NCI at fair value. Acquisition costs always go to P&L, never goodwill.
items.calculation:
consideration = 44000000
nci = 10500000
net_assets = 50000000
answer = consideration + nci - net_assets
check_notes: Checker: The question says 'Goodwill is?', which is slightly informal, but it is unambiguous.
Checker: The question states that NCI is measured at fair value, and this is redundant because the NCI fair value is already given. It is not a real problem.
Checker: The date 1 October 2026 is irrelevant, but that is harmless.
